title: Perishable Knowledge.
subtitle: 9 Laws for Becoming Irreplaceable
hero_blurb: Everyone is asking the same question: how do I stay valuable in a world that knows everything? The answer is older than AI. Based on the popular Stanford University course, here are nine laws for finding your edge.
waitlist_note: Waitlist subscribers get early chapters, notes from the margins, and first word when pre-orders open.
argument_heading: Success has never belonged to the smartest person in the room. Not before AI — and not now.
argument_paragraphs: I have been answering one question for years at the Stanford Graduate School of Business, in the packed class where companies like DoorDash, Zūm, and Guild Education were born: how do I stay valuable in a world that knows everything? My students arrive believing their job is to out-smart everyone. They leave knowing something better.

Every breakthrough starts the same way. Someone — a Marie Curie, a Henry Ford, a Steve Jobs — spots something many brilliant people missed and acts on it before the window closes. I call it _perishable knowledge_, and it can't be Googled or generated, because it doesn't exist until someone discovers it. And it spoils: the moment an insight is revealed, it starts turning into static knowledge, the kind anyone can look up, and the edge is gone.

I have made millions following its nine laws — and lost millions ignoring them. The book teaches all nine, following the lifecycle of a perishable insight: how to find one worth having, how to capture the value while it's live, and how to let go before it costs you.

Applicable to any industry, experience level, or career stage, _Perishable Knowledge_ is more than proof that humans still matter in the age of AI. It's proof that winning was never reserved for the smartest person in the room. You don't have to be a genius. You have to see the right insights first.

author_note_heading: A short note from the author.
author_note_paragraphs: I have spent the last decade on both sides of the table — first building companies, then picking them. In that time, one pattern kept showing up in the founders who outperformed the rest. It wasn't grit, or taste, or any of the usual explanations. It was how they handled information that was about to stop being true.

I started writing _Perishable Knowledge_ as a newsletter because I wanted to think out loud about what that looked like. The book is what happens when you follow a good question for four years and discover it is bigger than you thought.
